L’indice de chaleur (nom original en ang: The heat index (original English name: Heat Index (HI) or humidity) is an index developed in the United States.

The heat index (originally known in English as the Heat Index (HI) or “humiture”) is an index developed in the United States. It combines the ambient air temperature and relative humidity, in shaded areas, to estimate how the human body perceives the temperature—that is, how much hotter it would feel if the relative humidity were at a different level in the shade. The result is also known as the “feels-like temperature” or “apparent temperature.” For example, when the temperature is 32°C (or 90°F) with 70% relative humidity, the heat index is 41°C (or 106°F). This heat index temperature has an implied (unspecified) humidity of 20%. This is the relative humidity value at which the heat index formula indicates that 41°C is felt as 41°C. A heat index temperature of 32°C has an implied relative humidity of 38%.
L’indice de chaleur est basé sur la capa: The heat index is based on the human body’s ability to cool the skin by producing sweat.

The heat index is based on the human body’s ability to cool the skin by producing sweat. As sweat evaporates into the air, it draws energy from the environment, lowering the temperature of the boundary layer in contact with the skin and creating a sensation of coolness. As the relative humidity of the air increases, evaporation becomes less efficient, resulting in a subjective sensation of increased heat. This index should not be confused with the Canadian humidex, which uses a different formula to quantify the same effect.
